SECTION 010:00–4:01

Undo a product in reverse order

Associativity lets inverse pairs meet; factor order still matters.

Lecture 4 turns the steps of elimination into a factorization of the original matrix. First, Strang establishes the algebra needed to move a product of elimination matrices to the other side of an equation.

Suppose A and B are invertible square matrices of the same size. Their product is invertible, and

(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

Check this on the right by bringing the middle inverse pair together:

(AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹ = AIA⁻¹ = I.

Check the other side as well:

(B⁻¹A⁻¹)(AB) = B⁻¹(A⁻¹A)B = B⁻¹IB = I.

The parentheses can move because multiplication is associative. The factors themselves stay in order. Acting on a vector, AB applies B first and A second. To undo that sequence, apply A⁻¹ first and B⁻¹ second; written as a matrix product, that is B⁻¹A⁻¹.

Extend the same rule

(ABC)⁻¹ = C⁻¹B⁻¹A⁻¹. Reverse the order and invert every factor.

SECTION 024:01–6:44

Transpose and inverse can be taken in either order

A transpose reverses a product, too.

Transposing exchanges a matrix’s rows and columns. It also reverses the order of multiplication:

(AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.

Start with AA⁻¹ = I and transpose both sides. The identity is unchanged by transposition, so

(A⁻¹)ᵀAᵀ = I.

Transposing A⁻¹A = I also gives Aᵀ(A⁻¹)ᵀ = I. Thus (A⁻¹)ᵀ is the inverse of Aᵀ:

(Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ.

For a single invertible matrix, either sequence works: invert and then transpose, or transpose and then invert. This does not say that arbitrary matrix factors can be interchanged. The order reversal in the transpose rule is exactly what makes the argument work.

These identities will be used repeatedly as the course moves from row operations to the structure of matrices.

SECTION 036:44–10:22

Eliminate a two-by-two matrix

One multiplier turns A into U.

For now, assume elimination can proceed with nonzero pivots and no row exchanges. Strang begins with

A=[2187]

The first pivot is 2. To remove the 8 below it, use the multiplier 8/2 = 4:

R₂ ← R₂ − 4R₁.

The second row becomes (8, 7) − 4(2, 1) = (0, 3). Writing the row operation as left multiplication gives

[10−41][2187]=[2103]

This gives E₂₁A = U. The subscript identifies the entry being removed: row 2, column 1. The minus sign in E₂₁ records subtraction of the multiplier times the first row.

The resulting matrix U is upper triangular. Its diagonal entries, 2 and 3, are the pivots. If the original bottom-right entry had been 4 instead of 7, the last row would have become zero and the matrix would have been singular. Strang chooses 7 to keep both pivots nonzero.

SECTION 0410:22–13:32

Put A on its own: A = LU

L restores the eliminated entry; D can store the pivots separately.

Multiply E₂₁A = U by E₂₁⁻¹ on the left. The original matrix is now written as a product:

[2187]=[1041][2103]

The new factor L = E₂₁⁻¹ is lower triangular. It has ones on its diagonal and the positive multiplier 4 below the diagonal. It adds back four copies of the first row, recovering (8, 7) from (0, 3).

Check the product by rows: row 1 stays (2, 1), while row 2 becomes 4(2, 1) + (0, 3) = (8, 7). Thus A = LU records the same elimination in a different form.

Pull the pivots into a diagonal matrix

The pivots in U can be separated into D = diag(2, 3). Divide each row of U by its pivot to obtain a unit upper triangular factor, here called U₀:

[2103]=[2003][11/201]
A = LDU₀. Both L and U₀ have diagonal entries equal to 1.

In the LU convention, U contains the pivots. In the LDU convention, D contains them. These are two ways to store the same calculation; the lecture mainly uses LU.

SECTION 0513:32–17:10

Track the order in a three-by-three elimination

The first row operation appears at the right of the product.

For a three-by-three matrix, ordinary elimination first removes entry (2, 1), then entry (3, 1), and finally entry (3, 2). Each operation uses the matrix produced by the previous one.

A → E₂₁A → E₃₁E₂₁A → E₃₂E₃₁E₂₁A = U.

The rightmost elementary matrix acts first. To solve this matrix equation for A, invert the whole product. The inverse-of-a-product rule from the opening section gives

A = E₂₁⁻¹E₃₁⁻¹E₃₂⁻¹U.
L = E₂₁⁻¹E₃₁⁻¹E₃₂⁻¹.

Every inverse is easy: change the sign of the single elimination multiplier. The order of these inverses is essential. It is the reversal of the written product that acted on A.

Why prefer L to the product E = E₃₂E₃₁E₂₁? Both describe elimination, but L has a simpler relationship to the multipliers. The next example shows why.

SECTION 0617:10–20:17

Why the combined elimination matrix contains a 10

A later row operation carries an earlier row change along with it.

Strang uses two elementary matrices, taking E₃₁ = I because no operation in position (3, 1) is needed:

[1000100−51][100−210001]=[100−21010−51]

The entry 10 in the bottom-left corner is correct, even though neither individual matrix has a 10. The first operation replaces row 2 by R₂ − 2R₁. The second subtracts five copies of that updated row from row 3:

R₃ − 5(R₂ − 2R₁) = R₃ − 5R₂ + 10R₁.

The product therefore records a combined effect on the original rows. Its bottom row is (10, −5, 1). That 10 is the product of the two linked multipliers, with a positive sign from two subtractions.

The elimination matrix E remains lower triangular with ones on its diagonal, but its entries need not simply be the negatives of the original multipliers. This is the inconvenience that the L factor avoids.

SECTION 0720:17–26:06

The multipliers go directly into L

Inverting the product removes the unwanted interaction.

Now invert the combined operation, reversing the order:

[100210001][100010051]=[100210051]

This product is L. Its (3, 1) entry is zero; no extra 10 appears. The multipliers 2 and 5 sit at positions (2, 1) and (3, 2), exactly where elimination used them.

More generally, when elimination finishes without row exchanges, L has ones on the diagonal and the elimination multiplier ℓij in each position below it. Each multiplier is the current entry being eliminated divided by its pivot.

Two descriptions of the same work

EA = U describes the operations that remove entries. A = LU stores the multipliers in L and the resulting rows in U.

This also explains the practical storage idea in the lecture. As elimination proceeds, save the multipliers and the rows of U. The original entries of A no longer need to be kept separately: its information is preserved by the two factors.

The “no row exchanges” assumption matters. Once rows are exchanged, their ordering must also be recorded. Permutation matrices, introduced at the end of the lecture, provide that record.

SECTION 0826:06–33:53

Count the work in one elimination stage

A dense trailing square is updated at each pivot.

How much more work does a larger system require? Strang considers a dense n × n matrix, so there are no useful zeros that let us skip most of the updates.

The typical update multiplies a pivot-row entry by a multiplier and subtracts it from another entry:

aᵢⱼ ← aᵢⱼ − ℓᵢₖaₖⱼ.

The lecture counts a multiplication followed by a subtraction together as one update. Counting the arithmetic operations separately doubles the leading count.

For a 100 × 100 matrix, the first stage fixes the first column and updates the remaining entries. The next stage works on a smaller problem. The rough costs are 100², then 99², then 98², and so on.

More precise indexing. If we count only trailing-entry multiply–subtract updates, stage k changes an (n − k) × (n − k) block. For n = 100, the first such block has 99² entries. Computing the multipliers also takes divisions. These details change lower-order terms, while preserving the lecture’s leading cubic estimate.

SECTION 0933:53–38:35

Why the leading cost is one-third n cubed

Adding shrinking squares produces a cubic total.

Adding the rough stage counts gives

n² + (n − 1)² + ··· + 2² + 1² ≈ n³/3.

There are n terms, each at most n², so the total is at most n³. The smaller terms account for the factor one-third. Strang connects that coefficient with the integral of x², whose antiderivative is x³/3.

Consequently, doubling n costs about eight times as much factorization work for large dense matrices. The lecture’s count is a leading-term estimate, rather than an exact count of every division and subtraction.

Keep the counting convention visible

About n³/3 multiply–subtract pairs
or about 2n³/3 separate arithmetic operations.
Exact update count. Counting only the trailing-entry updates described in the previous section gives ∑r=1n−1 r² = n(n − 1)(2n − 1)/6. Its leading term is n³/3. For n = 100 this is 328,350 pairs, before divisions and other work. This exact formula is an editorial refinement of the lecture’s estimate.

Strang contrasts elimination with a factorial-cost determinant approach. That comparison concerns direct expansion of determinants; determinants can also be computed by elimination. The cubic estimate here concerns dense Gaussian elimination.

SECTION 1038:35–40:19

Reuse the factors for each right-hand side

Pay for the factorization once, then solve triangular systems.

All the expensive work so far was on the coefficient matrix A. Carrying a single right-hand-side vector b through elimination costs much less because it has just one column.

Once A = LU is available, rewrite Ax = b as LUx = b. Set c = Ux and solve in two stages:

Lc = b   →   Ux = c.

The first is forward substitution through a lower triangular matrix with diagonal entries 1. The second is back substitution through U. Together they require roughly n² multiply–subtract pairs, plus lower-order work.

If the same matrix is used with several different right-hand sides, keep L and U. Each new b needs those triangular solves, rather than a new factorization.

One factorization: about n³/3 pairs.
Each right-hand side: about n² pairs.
Explicit solve interpretation. The lecture states the lower cost for b and describes reuse of LU. The notation Lc = b followed by Ux = c spells out that procedure. Counting multiply and subtract separately gives leading costs 2n³/3 and 2n², respectively.

SECTION 1140:19–45:17

Row exchanges are permutation matrices

Rearrange the identity’s rows to describe a rearrangement of any matrix.

A zero in a pivot position can require exchanging rows. This need not mean the matrix is singular; a useful nonzero pivot may be available in a lower row. To record row reordering, use a permutation matrix P.

Construct P by rearranging the rows of the identity. Left multiplication by P applies the same rearrangement to the rows of A. For example,

P12=[010100001]

For three rows, there are six possible permutations. One keeps every row fixed. Three exchange a pair of rows. The remaining two move all three rows in opposite cycles.

For example, the matrix with rows (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1), and (1, 0, 0) produces the row order (R₂, R₃, R₁). The figure displays the full list, following Strang’s enumeration.

Every permutation matrix has exactly one 1 in each row and each column, with all other entries zero. This guarantees that every input row appears once in the output.

SECTION 1245:17–47:57

Invert permutations by transposing

Composing or undoing row reorderings stays within the same family.

Multiplying two permutation matrices composes two row reorderings, so the result is another permutation matrix. Undoing a row reordering also gives a permutation matrix. Together with the identity, these operations form the permutation group discussed at the end of the lecture.

A single swap is its own inverse: swapping rows 1 and 2 twice restores the starting order. A three-cycle is different. Its inverse is the cycle in the opposite direction.

P⁻¹ = Pᵀ,   so   PᵀP = PPᵀ = I.

To see why transposition works, note that the columns of P are the standard basis vectors in some order. Each has dot product 1 with itself and 0 with the others. Those dot products are precisely the entries of PᵀP.

There are 3! = 6 ways to order three rows and 4! = 24 ways to order four rows. In general, n rows have n! permutations: n choices for the first row, then n − 1 for the next, continuing down to 1.

Explanation and next step. The dot-product proof and general n! count expand the lecture’s stated inverse rule and counts for three and four rows. Strang leaves the use of permutations in elimination for the next lecture. The A = LU discussion above assumes no row exchanges.
